longForm.title: The Combined Action Platoon: The War the Marine Corps Was Fighting in the Villages
longForm.excerpt: While Westmoreland ran search-and-destroy operations in the highlands, the Marine Corps embedded small units in Vietnamese villages in I Corps. The Combined Action Platoon program produced results that conventional operations did not. It was never large enough to matter at scale.
paragraphs: The Marine and the Vietnamese Popular Force soldiers have been living in the same village for seven months. He knows the family across the canal, and the elder who runs the hamlet committee, and the names of two Viet Cong — knows them because they are from families who have been in this place for generations, same as the people who are not Viet Cong. The infrastructure is not a mystery. It is a neighborhood. This is what the Combined Action Platoon program looks like from inside it: not a counterinsurgency theory but a daily argument about who belongs where, conducted in a language most of the Marines are still learning.

The CAP concept developed in I Corps — the five northernmost provinces of South Vietnam, the Marine Corps' area of responsibility — in 1965, during the same months that General Westmoreland was building the large-unit search-and-destroy architecture that would define American strategy for the next three years. The Marine Corps, led in the Pacific by General Victor Krulak and in III Marine Amphibious Force by General Lewis Walt, had a different read on the war. Their argument was simple and not popular at MACV: the war would be won or lost among the South Vietnamese population, not in the jungle engagements that search-and-destroy produced. An enemy who could draw from a sympathetic population for recruits, logistics, and intelligence was an enemy who could sustain losses indefinitely. The way to defeat that enemy was to deny him the population — not by sweeping through it and moving on, but by living in it.

A Combined Action Platoon consisted of approximately fifteen Marines and a Navy corpsman assigned to work alongside thirty-four South Vietnamese Popular Forces — the local militia organized at the village level. The Marines lived in the village. They ate what the villagers ate, slept where the villagers slept, and went out on patrol with the PF on the trails and rice paddy dikes that the PF had walked their whole lives. They were not guests who came and went. They were, to the degree that a foreign force with a language barrier can be, residents. The theory was that an American presence embedded in the village, combined with a Vietnamese force that already understood the local social geography, could provide security that a passing infantry company could not — because the passing infantry company left, and the Viet Cong came back.

The tactical reality of life in a CAP village was violent in a specific way. CAP units were small, isolated, and without the quick reaction force that a conventional battalion had on call. When the Viet Cong attacked a CAP village — which they did regularly, often at night, with mortar fire and ground assault — the Marines and PF were on their own until helicopter support arrived. The casualty rate in the Combined Action Program was high. The Marines who volunteered for it — it was a volunteer assignment — understood they were trading the relative safety of a large unit for the operational freedom and relationships that small unit embedded work allowed. The record of individual CAP engagements is documented in Marine Corps historical accounts that are detailed and specific about what it cost: ambushes on patrol, mortar attacks on the perimeter, sappers probing the wire at 0300.

The political conflict that ran underneath the CAP program was the argument between Krulak and Westmoreland that MACV's official positions never quite resolved. Westmoreland needed Marine battalions for the large-unit operations in the highlands and the DMZ area. Marines in individual-size embedments in delta and coastal villages were Marines not available for Operation HARVEST MOON or the battles along the DMZ. Krulak argued that search-and-destroy was producing tactical results — engagements won, body counts — and strategic stalemate, because the villages from which the NVA and VC drew their support remained contested or enemy-controlled. Westmoreland argued that destroying the NVA's main force units was the prerequisite for everything else. The argument went to the JCS and to Robert McNamara, and MACV's position prevailed. The CAP program remained small — never more than a few percent of the Marine Corps' Vietnam commitment — because the institutional preference for large-unit operations limited its resources.

In the villages where CAP units operated for extended periods, the results were measurable. Viet Cong access to the village — for taxation, recruiting, and intelligence — declined. Village-level governance strengthened. South Vietnamese Popular Forces, trained and mentored by the Marine NCOs and officers in the CAP, improved in tactical competence. The security that a CAP could provide was not absolute — Viet Cong mortar attacks on CAP villages happened throughout the program's life — but it was consistent in a way that a battalion sweep that moved on after three days was not. The CORDS program that Robert Komer built from 1967 applied similar logic at a larger scale, combining military and civilian resources in a coordinated pacification effort. By 1971-1972, the CORDS data showed significant improvements in hamlet security ratings across South Vietnam. The CAP was a precursor to and a model for that effort.

The limitation of the CAP program was scale. By 1968, the Marine Corps was running approximately 114 Combined Action Platoons covering a fraction of I Corps' villages. The delta provinces, which contained half of South Vietnam's population, were Army territory and the Army had no equivalent program. The villages that had CAP coverage were measurably more secure than those that did not. The villages that did not have CAP coverage were the majority. The program demonstrated that the approach worked. It did not demonstrate that the approach could be implemented at the scale the problem required within the time and resources available. That gap — between the proof of concept and the scale of application — is the consistent finding of retrospective analysis of the pacification effort in Vietnam.

The Marines who served in CAP units came home with a different experience of the war than the Marines who served in conventional infantry units — and a different kind of knowledge. They knew specific families in specific villages by name. They knew what the Viet Cong told the villagers about why the Americans were there, and they knew what the villagers actually believed, which was sometimes different and sometimes not. The program produced, in the people who went through it, a ground-level understanding of the political dimension of the conflict that conventional infantry service did not. Whether that understanding has shaped American counterinsurgency doctrine in subsequent decades is a question the doctrine itself does not entirely answer.

shortForm.title: Victor Krulak vs. William Westmoreland: The Argument That Defined American Strategy in Vietnam
shortForm.excerpt: In 1965, Victor Krulak told anyone who would listen that the war would be won or lost in the villages, not in the jungle. Westmoreland said the NVA's main force units were the target. MACV won the argument. Krulak was right.
paragraphs: The argument between Victor Krulak and William Westmoreland was not personal — they were professional officers making professional arguments about competing theories of how to win the same war. Krulak's position, articulated in a series of memoranda and briefings from 1965 through 1967, was that the war's center of gravity was the South Vietnamese population: control it, and the NVA and VC lost the support base that sustained them; fail to control it, and no number of jungle engagements would produce a strategic result. Westmoreland's position was that the NVA's main force units — the conventional military formations that could be located, fixed, and destroyed in set-piece battles — were the decisive element. Defeat them, and the guerrilla infrastructure would wither. Both men cited evidence for their positions. Both had evidence.

The institutional argument was resolved in Westmoreland's favor by the force structure available and the timelines expected. Large-unit search-and-destroy operations were what the Army and Marine Corps knew how to run. The CAP program required Marines who could operate in small isolated teams, learn enough Vietnamese to function in a village, and sustain the mission for months without the support infrastructure a conventional unit relied on. Training and selecting those Marines took time, and the Marines trained for it were unavailable for the operational priorities MACV was running simultaneously. Krulak's argument was strategically correct; Westmoreland's was institutionally executable. The institution chose what it could execute.

The retrospective assessments of both men's arguments have largely vindicated Krulak's analysis. The pacification programs that produced the most durable results — CORDS, the CAP, the Phoenix Program's village-level intelligence work — were built on the logic Krulak had been advancing since 1965. They matured in the early 1970s, when American political will to sustain the commitment was exhausting. The insight arrived at the right conclusion too late. The standard military history account frames the CAP-versus-attrition debate as a path not taken, with the implication that taking it would have changed the outcome. The more honest assessment is that taking it fully would have required a different American Army from the one that existed — differently trained, differently organized, differently motivated — and there was no mechanism for that transformation inside the timeline of the actual war.

onThisDay.headline: Mexican Artillery Besieges Fort Texas on the Rio Grande
onThisDay.body: On May 4, 1846, Mexican artillery continued its bombardment of Fort Texas on the north bank of the Rio Grande, while General Zachary Taylor's main American force marched from Point Isabel to relieve the garrison. Taylor's army would engage Mexican forces at the Battle of Palo Alto on May 8 and at Resaca de la Palma on May 9, in the opening conventional engagements of the Mexican-American War.
